opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's great to be here.

For me, the motivation really came from living on both sides of that line for a long time. Early in my career I was much closer to the research and data systems world, thinking about how to make things scale and run efficiently. Then at Meta I spent years working on PyTorch and the broader AI infrastructure around it. That experience taught me a lot about the gap between research and production.

On the research side, people want flexibility. They want to iterate fast, try new architectures, and not fight the tooling. PyTorch succeeded largely because it respected that. But once you take those models into production, the priorities flip. You care about latency, cost, reliability, and running at huge scale. My team spent an enormous amount of effort bridging those two worlds, and it was hard even inside a company with Meta's resources and expertise.

When generative AI started to take off, I saw that every company was about to hit that same wall, and most of them would not have a large in-house infrastructure team to get over it. Developers could prototype something amazing with a large model in an afternoon. Then they'd try to ship it and run into slow inference, unpredictable costs, and the complexity of customizing and serving models efficiently.

So the idea behind Fireworks was to take what we learned building infrastructure at that scale and make it available to everyone. We wanted to give developers the speed and flexibility they love from the research world together with production-grade performance and cost efficiency. We also wanted them to own and customize their models instead of being locked into one closed system. That combination of research-style velocity and production-grade systems is really the core of why we started the company.

r001.rationale: The response describes Lin’s Meta infrastructure work and how generative AI would create production challenges for companies, but it does not say that her Meta experience gave her confidence AI would bring a major industrial transformation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. It's great to be here.

I'd say my whole career has lived at that boundary between research and production systems, and honestly the tension between the two is what pushed me to start Fireworks.

I spent a number of years at Meta, where I led the PyTorch team and the broader AI infrastructure effort. PyTorch started as a research-first framework. Researchers loved it because it was flexible, eager, Pythonic, easy to iterate on. But the moment you tried to take that same model and run it at Meta scale, serving billions of people, you hit a completely different set of problems. Latency, cost, reliability, hardware utilization. Those are not the problems researchers wake up thinking about, and they shouldn't be. But somebody has to solve them, and the gap between a model that works in a notebook and a model that works in production was enormous.

So a lot of my work was essentially building bridges. How do you keep the experience that researchers need, while making the output deployable? That taught me two things. First, the infrastructure layer is where most of the value gets unlocked or lost. A great model that's too slow or too expensive to serve doesn't change anything. Second, the people who are best at building that layer are usually locked inside a handful of big companies, because that's where the scale problems exist.

When generative AI took off, I saw that gap about to repeat itself across the entire industry, but at a much larger scale. Suddenly every company wanted to build with these models, but almost none of them had the systems expertise to run them efficiently. Open models were getting good very quickly, and I believed strongly that developers would want to own and customize their models rather than just call a closed API. But doing that well requires exactly the kind of deep systems work I'd spent years on.

That felt like the moment. The motivation for Fireworks was really to take what we learned building AI infrastructure at scale inside Meta and make it available to every developer, so they can go from experimentation to production without building that whole stack themselves. The research side gave me conviction about where models were heading. The systems side gave me conviction that inference, speed, and cost would be the real bottleneck. Fireworks sits right at that intersection.

astra-6.text:
Moving between research and building systems taught me that a promising research result is really the beginning. Getting it into production—making it reliable, efficient, and easy for people to use—is a whole other challenge. And that work often reveals the next set of research questions.

That connection is what motivated me to start Fireworks AI. With generative AI, the models have become incredibly capable, but there’s still a lot of complexity between having access to a model and building a useful application. We wanted to make that path much simpler, so developers could focus on what they wanted to create while we handled the infrastructure needed to run the models well.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, research and building systems have always been closely connected. Research opens up new possibilities, but building a system forces you to ask what it takes to make those possibilities useful. Can people access it easily? Can it run reliably? Can you deliver the performance they need at a cost that makes sense?

Moving between those perspectives made me appreciate how much engineering sits between a promising model and an application people can actually use. And that work can become a barrier for developers who have a great idea but don’t want to build an entire AI infrastructure stack.

That was the motivation behind Fireworks AI: to make it easier for developers to take advances in generative AI and turn them into real applications. I see the systems work as a way to extend the impact of the research—to get those capabilities into more people’s hands.
